# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles 143 coordinate-anchored settlement trajectories (376 dated benchmark observations, averaging 2,63 per site with 62 holding three or more benchmarks) and 155 excluded records (298 total reviewed ledger candidates) across the Central Plains (USGS Hydrological Unit 11, 645.289 km²) from 9500BC to 1600AD across eight states (Oklahoma 50, Texas 46, Kansas 23, Arkansas 14, Louisiana 5, Colorado 3, New Mexico 1 and Missouri 1).

The archaeological sequence spans Palaeoindian bison-kill locales across the Llano Estacado breaks and High Plains (Miami, Cooper Bison Kill, Lipscomb, Folsom, Olsen-Chubbuck, Winger) [@holliday1997clovis], Woodland floodplain earthworks at Toltec Mounds (1.450 at 800AD) [@rolingson1998toltec], Caddoan mound complexes led by Spiro (3.100 at 1350AD), Battle Mound (1.650 at 1400AD), Carden Bottoms (1.450 at 1500AD), Battle Mound Caddo City (1.300 at 1500AD) and Hatchel (1.100 at 1450AD) [@brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo], Plains Village settlements at Antelope Creek-Alibates (1.200 at 1300AD) and Washita-Duncan (820 at 1400AD) [@lintz1986antelope; @drass1997washita] and coalescent Wichita towns led by Etzanoa (14k at 1600AD), Tobias-Quivira (3.600 at 1550AD), Tobias Great Bend Town (2k at 1600AD) and Spanish Fort Taovaya Town (1.500 at 1600AD) [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

# Background

Archaeological documentation across HU 11 bridges humid Arkansas-Red alluvial mound landscapes in the east and semi-arid High Plains canyons in the west [@wedel1959kansas; @brown1996spiro]. Early Holocene western sites (Miami from 9500 to 9200BC, Cooper Bison Kill from 9200 to 8400BC, Lipscomb from 8900 to 8600BC, Folsom from 8700 to 8300BC) capture specialised *Bison antiquus* procurement events adjacent to classic Llano Estacado Clovis localities [@holliday1997clovis].

In the eastern bottomlands, Plum Bayou mounds at Toltec Mounds (600 to 1000AD) evolved alongside Lower Mississippi Valley Middle Woodland centres [@toth1988marksville; @rolingson1998toltec] prior to Caddoan florescence along the Arkansas and Red rivers [@brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo]. Western Panhandle quarries at Antelope Creek-Alibates simultaneously channeled chert and maize across Southern Plains trade paths linked westward toward Upper Rio Grande frontier pueblos [@lintz1986antelope; @kessell1979pecos].

Following fifteenth-century abandonment of small Panhandle and Washita farmsteads, Arkansas-Walnut and Little Arkansas river terraces supported aggregated Wichita grass-lodge towns documented by Spanish entradas at 1541AD and 1601AD [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

# Methodology

## Inclusion Criteria and Demographic Reconstruction

All 298 documented candidates in the regional source ledger follow Operation Viscount attribution rules. Across the basin, 143 distinct coordinates pass spatial deduplication (8 High Plains, 103 Middle Arkansas and 32 Lower Arkansas), while 155 candidates are excluded: 154 duplicate-alias consolidations merged within 2 km of canonical sites (led by Battle Mound, Tobias-Quivira, Spiro, Alibates Ruin and Etzanoa) plus one unquantified non-habitation rockshelter at Sliding Slab Rock Shelter.

For the 143 included entries, population series integrate three independent evidentiary streams:

1. **Stone-Slab and Earthlodge Room Counts**: Excavated floor plans and household multipliers (5 to 7 persons per residential structure) at Antelope Creek-Alibates, Buried City, Washita-Duncan and Plains Village components [@lintz1986antelope; @drass1997washita; @wedel1959kansas].
2. **Mound-Plaza Catchment Areas**: Residential precinct density reconstructions across Toltec Mounds, Spiro, Harlan, Crenshaw, Battle Mound, Hatchel and Carden Bottoms [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].
3. **Chronicled League-and-Lodge Tallies**: Cross-checked 1541AD and 1601AD Spanish observations paired with Great Bend excavated lodge rings across Etzanoa, Tobias-Quivira, Tobias, Little River and Malone [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

All included entries carry CENTAUR provenance and subtract cleanly from rural radiocarbon suitability grids across every benchmark [@kelly2025].

# Testing and Validation

Gazetteer reconciliation passed all structural checks with zero errors as of 18 November 2026 GMT+0:

1. **Ledger Parity**: All 298 ledger entries (143 included, 155 excluded: 154 duplicate-alias merges within 2 km plus Sliding Slab Rock Shelter) reconcile without gaps against the compiled settlement gazetteer.
2. **Coordinate and Attribution Integrity**: All 143 trajectories hold WGS84 latitude and longitude coordinates (31,73 N to 38,68 N, 90,51 W to 104,58 W), positive integer populations across 376 observations and consistent CENTAUR provenance.
3. **Hierarchical Coherence**: Direct benchmark-dated settlement sums stay bounded below sub-regional totals across all 23 horizons, rising from 95 inhabitants (2,24% of 4.250) at 8000BC and 8.880 (5,79% of 153,5k) at 1200AD to 14.750 (9,32% of 158,2k) in 1300AD, 19.620 (12,26% of 160k) in 1500AD and 33.340 (26,67% of 125k) in 1600AD.

```{r tbl-gazetteer, results='asis'}
clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("Existing Verified ", "", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub(" / ", " and ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
}

fmt_coord <- function(cvec) {
  lat <- as.numeric(cvec[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(cvec[[2]])
  paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), " N, ", viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), " W")
}

fmt_yr_lbl <- function(yr) {
  if (yr < 0L) paste0(abs(yr), "BC") else paste0(yr, "AD")
}

reg_short <- list(
  cp_high_plains_upper_arkansas = "High Plains",
  cp_neosho_verdigris_washita_prairies = "Middle Arkansas",
  cp_arkansas_valley_ozark_spiro = "Lower Ark. and Spiro"
)

rows <- lapply(names(sett), function(sk) {
  sv <- sett[[sk]]
  p_vec <- unlist(sv$population)
  yrs <- as.integer(names(p_vec))
  p_vals <- as.numeric(p_vec)
  pk_idx <- which.max(p_vals)
  y_min <- min(yrs)
  y_max <- max(yrs)
  span_str <- if (y_min == y_max) fmt_yr_lbl(y_min) else paste0(fmt_yr_lbl(y_min), " to ", fmt_yr_lbl(y_max))
  data.frame(
    Settlement = clean_text(sv$name),
    Polity = clean_text(sv$country),
    SubRegion = reg_short[[sv$region_id]],
    Coords = fmt_coord(sv$coords),
    Span = span_str,
    PeakYear = fmt_yr_lbl(yrs[pk_idx]),
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_number(p_vals[pk_idx], 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
    pk_num = p_vals[pk_idx]
  )
})
df_gaz <- do.call(rbind, rows)
df_gaz <- df_gaz[order(-df_gaz$pk_num, df_gaz$Settlement), ]
df_gaz <- head(df_gaz, 45L)
df_gaz$pk_num <- NULL
rownames(df_gaz) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  df_gaz,
  "Top 45 settlements in the Central Plains (HU 11) gazetteer ordered by peak population (of 143 included).",
  c("Settlement", "State", "Sub-region", "Coordinates", "Span", "Peak Year", "Peak Pop."),
  list(label = "tab:cp-gazetteer", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Results

## Archaic Bison Hunts, Woodland Earthworks and Caddoan Mound Centres

Early Holocene sites on the High Plains caprock and panhandle breaks (Miami 30 at 9200BC, Cooper Bison Kill 40, Lipscomb 40, Folsom 55 at 8700BC, Olsen-Chubbuck 75 at 7500BC, Winger 65) document brief mobile bison-procurement camps prior to Middle Archaic riverine base camps at William Young (95 at 3200BC).

Between 600AD and 1450AD, the largest nucleated towns clustered along the Lower Arkansas and Red River corridors (Table \ref{tab:cp-gazetteer}). Plum Bayou earthwork builders established Toltec Mounds (1.450 at 800AD), prefiguring regional Caddoan mound-centre networks led by Harlan (980 at 1100AD), Crenshaw (980 at 1150AD) and Spiro (3.100 at 1350AD, 35,31 N, 94,57 W) [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro]. Downstream along the Red River Great Bend and Arkansas valleys, Battle Mound peaked at 1.650 in 1400AD, Battle Mound Caddo City reached 1.300 in 1500AD, Hatchel reached 1.100 in 1450AD, Roitsch hit 920 in 1400AD and Carden Bottoms crested at 1.450 in 1500AD [@perttula1992caddo].

```{r fig-sett, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(

  "fig:sett-central-plains"
)
```

## Wichita Coalescence and Western Caprock Contraction

During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, settlement gravity migrated onto the Middle Arkansas and Walnut prairies (Figure \ref{fig:hero-central-plains}). Etzanoa (37,06 N, 97 W) expanded dramatically across 1400AD to 1600AD (14k at 1600AD), accompanied across the Great Bend, Salt Fork and Red River corridors by Tobias-Quivira (3.600 at 1550AD), Tobias Great Bend Town (2k), Spanish Fort Taovaya Town (1.500), Tobias (1.400), Longest Wichita Town (1.200), Little River (1.180), Malone (1.100), Deer Creek (980) and Sharps Creek (950) [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

On the Canadian River caprock breaks of Middle Arkansas, Antelope Creek-Alibates peaked at 1.200 in 1300AD alongside Buried City (680 at 1300AD) before thinning by 1500AD [@lintz1986antelope], whereas on the High Plains proper Sopris (320 at 1050AD), Cramer (240 at 1250AD) and Bell (210 at 1180AD) gave way to the protohistoric Edwards I Fortified Village (350 in 1500AD rising to 550 in 1600AD). Across Middle Arkansas overall, direct benchmark-dated town counts climbed from 14.350 (19,93% of 72k) at 1500AD to 30.040 (52,7% of 57k) by 1600AD.

Out of 155 excluded source-ledger records, 154 are duplicate-alias consolidations merged within 2 km of canonical complexes and one is the excluded non-habitation rockshelter Sliding Slab Rock Shelter; Table \ref{tab:cp-excluded} reports the leading 30 excluded records.

```{r tbl-excluded, results='asis'}
cand <- ledger$candidates
excl <- cand[cand$status != "included", , drop = FALSE]
excl <- head(excl, 30L)
if (nrow(excl) > 0L) {
  df_excl <- data.frame(
    Candidate = clean_text(excl$name),
    State = clean_text(excl$country),
    Status = clean_text(excl$status),
    Reason = clean_text(excl$reason),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  rownames(df_excl) <- NULL
  viscount_table(
    df_excl,
    "Leading 30 of 155 excluded source-ledger candidates in the Central Plains (HU 11).",
    c("Candidate Site", "State", "Status", "Exclusion Reason"),
    list(label = "tab:cp-excluded", font_size = "scriptsize")
  )
}
```

# Limitations

Sprawling protohistoric Wichita towns (Etzanoa, Tobias-Quivira) carry broader headcount bounds than masonry-walled Antelope Creek compounds because grass-lodge clusters extended unevenly across kilometres of river terrace recorded in 1541AD and 1601AD Spanish itineraries [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

Small Washita River and Plains Woodland farmsteads lacking distinct architectural cores remain absorbed into the continental North American radiocarbon substratum [@drass1997washita; @kelly2025].
